summary:
Still Out There is a “where are they now” guide to NASA’s far-flung hardware, built as a 14-page illustrated PDF booklet and a 7-slide deck. It is a snapshot for 15 November 2026, three days before Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth.

What I developed: Its hook is that distance in space is really delay. The booklet shows how long a radio message takes to reach Voyager 1 and 2, New Horizons, Mars and the Moon, and gives a scoreboard of where each probe is today. It tells the Voyager story and profiles rovers, landers and moon buggies from the 1960s onward. It also has a printable “send a message” toy with a delay formula, a binary decoder and a classroom game.

How it meets the challenge: It introduces school-age space fans to the hardware and the science it made possible, from probes still travelling to machines that went quiet.

Why it matters: It turns abstract numbers into something you can feel, such as a hello that takes two days, and shows the patience and cleverness behind exploration.
details:
What it does and how it works

Still Out There is a print-and-present “where are they now” guide to NASA’s hardware in deep space and on other worlds. Its central idea is that distance in space is really delay. Every probe sits at a distance, and every distance is a signal time. The booklet turns that idea into a delay ladder chart, 24-hour clock graphics, and a scoreboard of Voyager 1 and 2, New Horizons and the silent Pioneers. It also includes a Hall of Hardware covering Moon reflectors, moon buggies, Mars rovers, Ingenuity, Galileo and Cassini. A printable “send a message” toy lets readers pick a probe, use the formula (delay in minutes = distance in AU × 8.317) to work out when their message arrives, and encode it in binary. A classroom “human delay line” game, a quiz and a glossary round it out. The 7-slide deck summarises the same story for presenting.

Benefits and intended impact

It gives school-age space fans a concrete way to feel scale: a hello to Voyager 1 takes two days. It also shows that missions can end in different ways, such as going silent, ending on purpose, or running with no power at all. The aim is to build curiosity about the engineering behind exploration, and the toy and game give teachers something hands-on.

Tools and methods

  • Python with ReportLab to build the PDF, with custom-drawn charts and illustrations, and the Poppins and DejaVu Sans fonts.
  • Web searches for current figures, including Voyager 1’s one-light-day date (18 Nov 2026, 10:16:07 UTC) and the Voyager 2 and New Horizons distances.
  • Claude’s Slides artifact tool for the deck, using HTML and CSS slide files.

Creativity

The story is anchored on a real, imminent milestone. Ideas like “one light-day is one full turn of the clock” and “Earth-Sun distance as one metre” make the numbers tangible. The toy turns the delay into something readers do for themselves.

Factors considered

  • A printed page can’t be live, so figures are dated snapshots with formulas readers can update.
  • Estimates, such as the Pioneer distances, are labelled as estimates.
  • Earth’s orbit shifts distances by up to about 8 light-minutes through the year.
  • The language and layout suit younger readers while staying accurate.
dataRefs: Where Are Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 Now?
